# Natural causes (naturalism about disease, weather, comets) (`natural_causes`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by eclipse_prediction, contagion_theory
- Core idea: Events such as disease, lightning, earthquakes, eclipses and comets follow regular causes that can be studied, predicted and sometimes prevented; they are not messages, punishments or the work of witches aimed at particular people. The strongest evidence is prediction and indifference: an eclipse can be calculated years ahead to the hour, lightning can strike exposed objects whether it is a church tower or a tree, plague kills the pious and the wicked in the same street. The framing that worked historically is 'secondary causes': God, Heaven or the gods work through a regular order of nature, and studying that order honours its author. The practical consequence is to stop looking for whom to blame and start looking for how it happens.
- Pitfalls:
  - Presenting naturalism as atheism; nearly all its historical champions were believers, and the atheist framing gets the player prosecuted
  - Claiming natural explanations one does not actually have ('comets are just dirty snowballs') without being able to predict anything
  - Denying that an omen means anything to a court whose astrologers and diviners are state officials is an attack on the regime's legitimacy
  - Believing medieval scholars explained everything by miracle; scholastic natural philosophy sought natural causes as a matter of principle
- History: mesopotamia: c. 750 BC onwards – eclipses and planetary events are computed in advance, yet still read as omens for the king; greece: c. 585 BC – Thales and the Milesians explain earthquakes and lightning without gods; c. 400 BC Hippocratic 'On the Sacred Disease': epilepsy is no more divine than any other illness; china: c. 250 BC – Xunzi: Heaven's course is constant; rain follows the rain sacrifice just as it would without it; c. 80 AD Wang Chong: thunder is fire, not Heaven's anger; india: 499 – Aryabhata explains a lunar eclipse by the earth’s shadow and a solar eclipse by the moon obscuring the sun; later Carvaka authors reject appeals to supernatural agency; rome: c. 55 BC – Lucretius, De rerum natura; c. 65 AD Seneca, Natural Questions, treats comets as bodies with regular paths; islamic: 11th c. – Ibn Sina discusses uplift and erosion in mountain formation; al-Biruni infers from alluvial sediments that parts of the Indian plains were once under water; europe: c. 1120 – Adelard of Bath and William of Conches defend the search for natural causes; 1577 Tycho shows a comet lies beyond the moon; 1705 Halley predicts a comet's return; 1752 Franklin shows lightning is electricity
- Read:
  - Hippocratic Corpus, On the Sacred Disease (c. 400 BC)
  - G. E. R. Lloyd, Magic, Reason and Experience (1979)
  - Wang Chong, Lun-Hêng (tr. Alfred Forke, 1907)
